newsitem.title: USA: Denison, Texas, water and sewer revs BBB-plus-S&P.
newsitem.headline: Denison, Texas, water and sewer revs BBB-plus-S&P.

text.p: NEW YORK, Sept 17 - Standard & Poor's Corp Tuesday said it has assigned its triple-B'-plus rating to Denison, Texas' waterworks and sewer system revenue refunding bonds series 1996.

Additionally, Standard & Poor's has affirmed its triple-B'-plus rating on the city's waterworks and sewer system revenue bonds series 1985 and its triple-A' rating on the city's waterworks and sewer system revenue bonds series 1989, 1992, 1994 (various insurers).
The rating assigned to Denison's revenue bonds reflects the following risks:
-- Higher than average monthly water and sewer rates,
These risks are offset by the following strengths:
-- Stable and adequate debt service coverage,
-- Regular rate increases in the past three years, and
-- Adequate water and sewer capacity for existing demands with minimal capital needs.

Employment is centered in a diverse array of manufacturing and service companies. Employment growth, driven primarily by trade and services, suffered slightly in the 1991-1992 recession (1% employment decline), but has increased to about 3% annually in 1993-1995. Moderate unemployment tracks the U.S. and Texas average rates and the county rate was 5% in 1995. Local wealth is about 75% of the U.S. average and appears to have declined from 1990 levels.

Monthly water and sewer rates, at $56 per 10,000 gallons, reflect investment in water and sewer capacity since 1988. The city has passed another 3.3% rate increase to be implemented in October 1996, bringing rates to $58. These rates are somewhat higher than the average for similarly sized Texas cities at $50 per month and may decrease ratesetting flexibility given low wealth levels.

Revenue bond debt service coverage has met or exceeded the city's internal target of 1.25 times (x) since 1987 ranging from 1.27x 1993 and 1.5x in 1995. Coverage of total fixed charges, including debt service paid to the Red River Authority and the Army Corps. of Engineers, was adequate at 1.3x in 1995. Water and sewer fund liquidity totaled $477,000 at fiscal year-end 1995, or about 56 days' expenses. In addition, restricted funds include $2.3 million available to fund future capital projects, if necessary.
Both the water and sewer systems have adequate treatment capacity to meet system peaks, and there are no plans for expansion in the near future.
The outlook reflects Denison's moderately growing service area economy, stable financial performance, and limited capital needs, Standard & Poor's said.
